lessonTitle: Ward Rounds, Review and Discharge Planning: Continuity and Safe Transitions

blocks.text: Mr D's discharge was booked for noon. At 11:40 the pharmacist notices that the draft letter says 'continue all home medicines', yet the ward chart shows his ramipril was stopped on day 2 for acute kidney injury. Nobody wrote the reason or the restart plan down, and his GP would have restarted it the next morning.

blocks.markdown: **What a ward round is for.** Each review answers four questions: *Is the patient better, the same or worse? Is the working diagnosis still right? What has to happen today, and by whom? Is the patient ready to go, and what will make going home safe?* You answer them from three sources in order: the patient (symptoms, examination), the **trends** (observations, fluid balance, results, medicines administered) and the plan from the previous review. Always re-examine; never copy yesterday's entry forward.

blocks.title: Trend
blocks.text: The direction and rate of change of a measurement over time compared with the patient's own baseline. A trend can signal deterioration or recovery long before a single value crosses a population threshold.

blocks.markdown: **Reading trends.** Look at the whole chart, not the latest column. Three observations each inside the 'normal' range may still show a falling blood pressure and a rising heart rate that together suggest bleeding or sepsis. Pair every trend with a cause and an action: improving inflammatory markers and temperature may justify reviewing intravenous antibiotics against your local antimicrobial policy; a rising creatinine needs a cause search and a medicine review. Interpret results against the patient's own baseline and against laboratory-specific reference intervals.

blocks.caption: A sustained value below about 0.5 mL/kg/h for 6 hours or more is a widely used marker of acute kidney injury (KDIGO urine-output criterion); check the exact criteria against current guidance.
NEWS2 scale 1 as published by the Royal College of Physicians. Scale 2 for SpO2 applies only to patients with a prescribed target of 88-92%. Verify the chart against your trust's current version.

blocks.title: Worked example 1: reading a three-day trend on the post-take round
blocks.prompt: Mr C, 71, was admitted with community-acquired pneumonia and has had 08:00 observations (all on air, alert) as follows. Day 1: RR 24, SpO2 93%, SBP 112, HR 108, temperature 38.7 C. Day 2: RR 20, SpO2 95%, SBP 118, HR 92, temperature 37.8 C. Day 3: RR 18, SpO2 96%, SBP 122, HR 84, temperature 37.2 C. CRP fell from 240 to 150 to 70 mg/L. Interpret the trend and decide the day-3 plan.

steps.text: Score each day using the chart. Day 1: RR 24 scores 2, SpO2 93% scores 2, SBP 112 scores 0, HR 108 scores 1, temperature 38.7 scores 1, air 0, alert 0: total 6.
Day 2: RR 20 scores 0, SpO2 95% scores 1, SBP 118 scores 0, HR 92 scores 1, temperature 37.8 scores 0: total 2. Day 3: all parameters score 0: total 0.

Interpretation: the aggregate falls from 6 to 2 to 0 while CRP falls and the patient reports less cough. Every component moves in the same direction, so this is consistent with response to treatment, not a coincidence of one reading.

Plan: confirm by re-examining the chest, review whether intravenous antibiotics can switch to oral and decide the total course length against local antimicrobial policy (check BNF and local guidance for agent and dose), stop routine hourly-style monitoring in favour of the standard schedule, and begin discharge planning including pneumonia follow-up advice.

blocks.answer: The patient is improving on every axis (NEWS2 6 to 2 to 0, CRP falling). Day 3 plan: examine, review IV-to-oral switch and course length per local policy, de-escalate monitoring and start discharge planning.

blocks.markdown: **Escalation.** NEWS2 is a prompt, not a replacement for judgement. Escalate whenever (a) the aggregate reaches the locally defined trigger (commonly 5 or more for urgent review and 7 or more for an emergency response in the NEWS2 framework, but follow your trust's policy), (b) any **single parameter** scores 3, (c) the trend worsens even if the aggregate is low, or (d) a nurse or relative is worried. Before calling, repeat the observations manually, check the patient (a rapid ABCDE), check what the patient has had (drugs, fluids, oxygen) and know the resuscitation and escalation status. Use a structured format, state your concern plainly and document the response and a review time.

blocks.title: Low score, real concern
blocks.text: A low NEWS2 does not exclude serious illness. Young patients compensate until late, and some conditions (for example early sepsis in the immunosuppressed, or spinal and neurological emergencies) may not move the score. Clinical concern always justifies escalation.

blocks.title: Worked example 2: a safe discharge summary for a patient with a COPD exacerbation
blocks.prompt: Mrs F, 72, was admitted for 4 days with an infective exacerbation of COPD. She was treated with a short oral corticosteroid course and antibiotics (both completed in hospital, per local guidance), her inhaler was changed after a technique review, her usual ACE inhibitor was continued, and a sputum culture is pending. Draft the discharge summary.

steps.text: Header and diagnoses: patient identifiers, admission and discharge dates, the principal diagnosis (infective exacerbation of COPD) and relevant secondary problems, with the responsible consultant and the author's contact.

Medication changes as a three-column list: started, changed, stopped, each with the reason and intended duration. Here: inhaler changed after technique review (state product and why); no steroid or antibiotic to continue; all other usual medicines unchanged. Every drug and dose in the letter must be reconciled against the drug chart and checked against BNF and local guidance.

Actions for the GP: review in about one week, check the inhaler technique, offer pulmonary rehabilitation and smoking-cessation support, update the COPD action plan. Name what is expected and by whom.

Pending results and safety-net: state that the sputum culture is pending, who will review it, and how the GP will be told. Give the patient and carer clear return advice (worsening breathlessness, change in sputum, fever, drowsiness) and tell them when to seek urgent help. Record the treatment escalation preferences discussed.

blocks.answer: A safe summary lists diagnoses, medication changes with reasons, specific follow-up tasks with owners, pending results and patient safety-net advice. It reaches the GP and the patient promptly, ideally on the day of discharge.

rows: Gives the GP the clinical story and coding
Follow-up actions with an owner and date
Absent or buried in the text
blocks.caption: Core elements of a safe discharge summary.

items: Check the discharge medicines against the admission list and the drug chart; justify every stop, start and change.
State the reason a medicine was stopped and whether and when it should be restarted.
Name pending results and who will review them.
Give the patient the same safety-net advice in plain language and confirm understanding.
Do not state any dose from memory: verify against current BNF, NICE and local guidance.

points: A ward round re-examines the patient and reads trends against the patient's own baseline; the whole chart matters more than the latest value.
NEWS2 is a prompt for escalation: use the aggregate, any single parameter scoring 3, worsening trends and clinical concern, and follow your local policy.
Before escalating, repeat observations, perform a rapid assessment, check treatments and the escalation plan, then communicate in a structured way and document.
A safe discharge summary lists diagnoses, medication changes with reasons, follow-up tasks with owners, pending results and safety-net advice.

questions.stem: On a ward round you review a patient's chart. Over 12 hours the heart rate has risen from 78 to 91 to 104/min and systolic pressure has fallen from 132 to 118 to 106 mmHg, while each individual value is within the range often labelled normal for adults. Which is the most appropriate response?

options.text: Regard the changes as a trend that needs a bedside review, a cause search (for example bleeding, sepsis or drug effect) and a shorter observation interval
Take no action because every value is within the usual reference range
Wait until the heart rate exceeds 110/min before reviewing
Record the readings as an error and repeat them in 24 hours

questions.correctOptionText: Regard the changes as a trend that needs a bedside review, a cause search (for example bleeding, sepsis or drug effect) and a shorter observation interval

distractorRationale.a: Correct: a coherent movement in two parameters from the baseline is a trend that warrants review even if single values appear acceptable.
distractorRationale.b: Ignores the direction and combination of changes.
distractorRationale.c: Applying a fixed single threshold delays recognition.
distractorRationale.d: Dismisses real data and delays care.

questions.explanation: Trends show deterioration earlier than single values. A rising heart rate with a falling blood pressure is a recognised pattern that suggests volume loss or sepsis and needs a bedside assessment and more frequent monitoring.

questions.stem: A patient on day 3 of intravenous antibiotics for leg cellulitis is afebrile, the erythema is receding, eating, has a NEWS2 of 0 and a falling CRP. What is the best action on the ward round?

options.text: Review the antibiotic against any microbiology results and local antimicrobial policy, considering an oral switch and a defined stop date
Continue intravenous antibiotics indefinitely until the CRP reaches zero
Stop all antibiotics immediately without reviewing the culture result
Increase the observation frequency because a low NEWS2 suggests an unreliable chart

questions.correctOptionText: Review the antibiotic against any microbiology results and local antimicrobial policy, considering an oral switch and a defined stop date

distractorRationale.a: Correct: a clinically improving patient should have the antimicrobial plan reviewed (review, switch, stop) according to culture results and local policy.
distractorRationale.b: No evidence supports continuing intravenous therapy until the CRP is zero.
distractorRationale.c: Stopping without checking culture or policy is unsafe.
distractorRationale.d: A low score in an improving patient does not suggest error.

questions.explanation: Antimicrobial stewardship expects a documented review at 48-72 hours with a decision to continue, switch route, narrow or stop. Improving observations, afebrile status and a falling CRP support an oral switch if the culture and policy allow; agents and durations must be checked against current BNF and local guidance.

questions.stem: Calculate the NEWS2 aggregate score (scale 1) for this patient: respiratory rate 22/min, SpO2 94% on air, systolic blood pressure 104 mmHg, heart rate 98/min, alert, temperature 38.4 C. Give the total score.
questions.explanation: Respiratory rate 22 scores 2, SpO2 94% scores 1, air scores 0, systolic 104 scores 1, heart rate 98 scores 1, alert scores 0 and temperature 38.4 C scores 1, giving a total of 6. A score of 5 or 6 is the usual trigger for an urgent clinical review in the NEWS2 framework, but confirm against your chart and local escalation policy.

questions.stem: A 75 kg man has a urinary catheter. The nurse records 300 mL of urine over the past 12 hours. Calculate his average urine output in mL/kg/h to two decimal places.
questions.explanation: Urine output = 300 mL / (12 h x 75 kg) = 0.33 mL/kg/h. This is below the widely used 0.5 mL/kg/h threshold, so the ward-round plan should treat oliguria as a problem: check catheter patency, assess volume status, review nephrotoxic drugs and consider acute kidney injury. Thresholds and fluid decisions must follow current KDIGO, NICE and local guidance.

questions.stem: A patient has respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 96% on air, systolic blood pressure 88 mmHg, heart rate 94/min, is alert and has a temperature of 36.6 C. The total NEWS2 is 4. What is the correct interpretation?

options.text: The single parameter scoring 3 (systolic pressure) calls for an urgent clinical review even though the aggregate is below 5
The aggregate of 4 means routine observations every 12 hours are sufficient
Because the total is under 5, escalation is not appropriate
The patient should be reviewed only if the heart rate rises above 110/min

questions.correctOptionText: The single parameter scoring 3 (systolic pressure) calls for an urgent clinical review even though the aggregate is below 5

distractorRationale.a: Correct: in the NEWS2 framework any single parameter scoring 3 triggers urgent review of the cause and the patient, regardless of the aggregate.
distractorRationale.b: Reduces monitoring in a hypotensive patient.
distractorRationale.c: Ignores the red-score rule and the clinical picture.
distractorRationale.d: Waits for further deterioration instead of acting on current hypotension.

questions.explanation: The aggregate can hide a single critical derangement. Systolic pressure of 88 mmHg scores 3 and demands a bedside review of cause (volume loss, sepsis, drugs, cardiac) and monitoring changes, according to local escalation policy.

questions.stem: Which item is essential in a discharge summary for the general practitioner?

options.text: A list of medicines started, changed and stopped, with the reason for each change
A copy of the complete handwritten ward-round notes for the whole admission
Only the final diagnosis, because details are in the hospital record
The consultant's views on the staffing of the ward

questions.correctOptionText: A list of medicines started, changed and stopped, with the reason for each change

distractorRationale.a: Correct: medication changes with reasons are the most error-prone element at transitions.
distractorRationale.b: Too long and unselective; the key information gets lost.
distractorRationale.c: Omits actions the GP must carry out.

questions.explanation: Discharge summaries must tell the receiving clinician what changed in the patient's medicines and why, together with diagnoses, follow-up tasks and pending results. Omitted or unexplained medication changes are a leading cause of harm after discharge.

questions.stem: A man is being discharged with a blood culture still awaiting a final result. What is the safest handling in the summary?

options.text: State the pending result, name the clinician responsible for reviewing it, and tell the GP how they will be informed of an abnormal result
Omit the pending test because the result is unknown
Ask the patient to phone the laboratory for the result next week
Leave a note in the ward folder only

questions.correctOptionText: State the pending result, name the clinician responsible for reviewing it, and tell the GP how they will be informed of an abnormal result

distractorRationale.a: Correct: pending results need an owner and a communication route so they are not lost.
distractorRationale.b: Pending tests silently disappear if not documented.
distractorRationale.c: Transfers responsibility to the patient and risks missed results.
distractorRationale.d: The GP cannot see a ward folder.

questions.explanation: Results pending at discharge are a recognised safety gap. Naming the test, the responsible person and the communication route ensures an abnormal result triggers action.

questions.stem: A low NEWS2 total means a patient who the nurse is worried about does not need escalation.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Clinical concern is an independent reason to escalate, because NEWS2 may not capture every serious illness. The score supports, but does not replace, clinical judgement.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man is on day 2 of treatment for pyelonephritis. Over the last 12 hours his heart rate has risen from 88 to 118/min, his systolic pressure has fallen from 124 to 96 mmHg, his urine output has fallen, and the nurse says he is newly confused. Explain how you would assess and escalate this, and what you would document.
markingGuide: Recognise a deteriorating trend in several parameters and possible sepsis with hypoperfusion; go to the bedside promptly
Repeat the observations manually, perform a rapid ABCDE assessment, check blood glucose, review fluid balance, medicines given and any oxygen

Check the escalation and resuscitation status and the local sepsis pathway; arrange urgent tests (bloods including lactate and cultures per policy) and start time-critical treatment per local guidance
Escalate immediately to a senior doctor, using the local escalation route, with a structured and concise message: the patient, the trend, your assessment, and what you need
Set a review time and monitoring frequency, inform the nurse in charge, and consider a higher level of care
Document the findings, the time of escalation, who was informed, the plan and the review time; do not state doses without BNF or local guidance
questions.explanation: A good answer moves from recognition (multi-parameter trend), through rapid assessment and checks, to timely senior escalation, with documented review and safety-netting. Marks are awarded for prompt senior involvement and for not delaying the bedside review.

questions.stem: Mr G, 77, was admitted with atrial fibrillation with a fast ventricular rate. By day 5 his rate is controlled, he has started an anticoagulant and a rate-limiting medicine, an existing antihypertensive was stopped because of low blood pressure, and an echocardiogram report is awaited. Outline the medication, follow-up and safety-net content of his discharge summary.
markingGuide: Medication list with started, changed and stopped drugs, each with a reason and intended duration; the stopped antihypertensive has a documented reason and a plan to review restart
Doses, indication and monitoring requirements for the new drugs stated and reconciled against the drug chart and checked against BNF and local guidance
Follow-up tasks with owner and timeframe: GP review of heart rate, blood pressure and renal function, anticoagulation counselling, outpatient or cardiology follow-up as needed
Pending echocardiogram result named with who will review it and how the GP will be informed
Patient safety-net advice in plain language: palpitations, bleeding, dizziness or fainting, stroke symptoms and who to contact; confirm understanding
questions.explanation: The summary should make every medicine change traceable, give the receiving clinician clear tasks and pending-result ownership, and prepare the patient to recognise problems early. Unexplained or undocumented changes are the commonest source of post-discharge error.
